nameStory: The fairy ring marasmius gets its enchanting name from its habit of growing in mysterious circles or arcs called fairy rings. Folk tales claimed these perfect circles were where fairies danced at night, leaving behind a ring of mushrooms as evidence of their midnight revelry. The scientific name 'oreades' refers to the mountain nymphs of Greek mythology, connecting this humble lawn mushroom to ancient stories of woodland spirits.
description: The fairy ring marasmius is a small, sturdy mushroom that pops up in grassy areas throughout New England. It has a tan to buff-colored cap that's about 1-2 inches across, sitting atop a tough, wiry stem. What makes this mushroom special is its ability to dry out completely during drought, then spring back to life when moisture returns. You'll often find them growing in distinctive circles or curved lines across lawns, fields, and grassy meadows.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Bell-shaped when young, flattening to a broad dome with a small bump in the center. Tan to buff colored, smooth and dry to the touch, often with subtle radial lines visible from the center to the edges.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Widely spaced, thick gills that are cream to pale tan colored. They're attached to the stem but don't run down it, and you can feel their substantial, almost leathery texture.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Remarkably tough and wiry, like thin rope. Tan to brown colored, hollow inside, and so flexible you can tie it in a knot without breaking it. No ring around the stem.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White to cream colored when you place the cap gill-side down on dark paper overnight.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, sweet smell often described as almond-like or reminiscent of fresh hay. Some people detect a faint garlic note.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Almost always grows in distinctive arcs, circles, or lines across grassy areas. The mushrooms seem to march in formation across lawns and fields.

habitat: Look for fairy ring marasmius in grassy areas throughout New England - lawns, parks, meadows, and field edges are prime spots. They prefer areas with rich, well-drained soil and plenty of organic matter in the grass roots. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations, thriving in both rural pastures and suburban yards where they often frustrate homeowners by creating dark green rings in the grass.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin in late spring after warm rains, with small flushes appearing in established fairy ring locations from previous years.
seasonality.summer: Peak season arrives with summer rains and humidity. Fresh mushrooms pop up regularly in fairy rings, especially after thunderstorms bring moisture to dry grass.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting strongly through early fall, often producing some of the largest and most numerous flushes before the first hard frost ends the season.
seasonality.winter: No visible mushrooms during New England winters, but the underground mycelium remains alive and ready to produce new fairy rings come spring.

funFact: Fairy ring marasmius mushrooms are nature's ultimate survivors - they can completely shrivel up and look dead during dry spells, then magically spring back to their full, plump shape within hours of getting wet, like tiny fungal resurrection plants!
confusionNotes: This mushroom can be confused with several toxic species that also grow in grassy areas, including the deadly poisonous Chlorophyllum molybdites (green spored parasol) which also forms fairy rings. The key difference is spore color - fairy ring marasmius has white spores while the dangerous look-alike has green spores. Memory trick: 'White spores might be right, green spores stay away clean.' Always check spore prints and never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification.
contextualKnowledge: The common name 'fairy ring champignon' can be misleading since many different mushroom species create fairy rings, and some of those are deadly poisonous. The term 'Scotch bonnet' is also confusing because it refers to both this edible species and some toxic mushrooms. When discussing fairy rings with others, always use the full scientific name to avoid dangerous mix-ups.
compareHints: Fairy ring marasmius stands out from other Marasmius species by its robust size and grassland habitat - most of its relatives are tiny and grow on dead wood or leaves. The collared parachute has a distinctive collar around its stem and grows on twigs, while the orange pinwheel is much smaller and bright orange. Fairy ring marasmius is the only common Marasmius in New England that regularly fruits in open grassy areas rather than forests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Marasmius relatives in New England, the collared parachute is distinguished by its unique gill-to-collar attachment and preference for small woody debris.
Among its Marasmius relatives, Hair-stemmed Pinwheel is distinguished by being both the smallest and having the thinnest stems.
